title: Sociocultural approach: social identity and influence
summary: Social identity theory, social learning theory, cognitive dissonance, conformity and compliance techniques.

keyterms.definition: Tajfel & Turner (1979): part of our self-concept comes from group membership, which motivates in-group favouritism.
Treating members of one's own group more positively than members of other groups.
Assigning people to groups on trivial criteria to test whether categorization alone causes in-group bias.
Bandura: behaviour is learned by observing and imitating models, influenced by attention, retention, reproduction and motivation.
Learning that a behaviour is rewarded by seeing a model rewarded for it.
Festinger: discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against one's beliefs, which people try to reduce.
Changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group, due to real or imagined pressure.
Conforming to be accepted or avoid rejection.
Conforming because we believe others know better.
A strategy for getting someone to agree to a request, e.g. foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-ball.

lessons.title: Social identity, social learning and dissonance

questions.prompt: In Tajfel et al. (1971), schoolboys were split into groups based on supposed preferences for Klee or Kandinsky. When allocating points, they often:
options: Maximised joint profit for both groups
Maximised the difference in favour of their own group
Gave all points to the other group
questions.explanation: Even trivial groups produced in-group favouritism, supporting social identity theory.

questions.prompt: In Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961), which children showed the most imitative aggression?
options: Those who saw a non-aggressive model
Those who saw an aggressive model
questions.explanation: Observing an adult hit a Bobo doll led to imitation, supporting social learning theory.

questions.statement: In Festinger and Carlsmith (1959), participants paid $1 to say a boring task was fun later rated it as more enjoyable than those paid $20.
questions.explanation: With little justification, they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

questions.statement: Social identity theory says in-group bias only happens when groups compete for resources.
questions.explanation: The minimal group studies showed categorization alone can be enough; competition is the focus of realistic conflict theory.

questions.text: Seeing a model rewarded and then copying the behaviour involves ___ reinforcement.
questions.explanation: In SLT, observed consequences shape motivation to imitate.

questions.text: According to SIT, comparing our group favourably with others boosts our self-___.
questions.explanation: Positive distinctiveness of the in-group enhances self-esteem.

questions.prompt: Match each SLT process to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Bandura proposed all four are needed for imitation.

questions.prompt: A limitation of Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) is that:
options: Hitting a doll may not reflect real aggression towards people
questions.explanation: The Bobo doll is designed to be hit, so ecological validity is limited.

questions.prompt: A smoker who knows smoking is harmful says "my grandad smoked and lived to 90". This is:
questions.explanation: Adding a consonant belief reduces the discomfort of conflicting cognitions.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of social identity theory.
questions.explanation: Tajfel and Turner describe categorization, identification and comparison.

questions.prompt: In Asch's line-judgement studies, about what proportion of responses on critical trials conformed to the wrong majority?
questions.explanation: Around a third of critical responses conformed; about a quarter of participants never conformed.

questions.prompt: Asch found conformity dropped sharply when:
options: One confederate gave the correct answer
questions.explanation: A single ally broke the unanimity of the group.

questions.statement: Bond and Smith (1996) found higher conformity in collectivist cultures in their meta-analysis of Asch-type studies.
questions.explanation: This links conformity to cultural dimensions.

questions.statement: Informational social influence is conforming to be liked.
questions.explanation: That is normative influence; informational influence is conforming because others may be right.

questions.text: Asking for a small favour first, then a larger one, is the foot-in-the-___ technique.
questions.explanation: Freedman & Fraser (1966) found people who agreed to a small request were much more likely to accept a large one.

questions.text: In the door-in-the-face technique, a large request is refused, then a ___ request is made.
questions.explanation: Cialdini et al. (1975) explained this through reciprocal concessions.

questions.prompt: Match each compliance technique to its study.
questions.explanation: Each exploits a different principle: consistency, reciprocity or commitment.

questions.prompt: In the low-ball technique, a person:
options: Is asked for something outrageous first
Agrees to a deal, then the cost is raised
Is asked for a tiny favour first
questions.explanation: Having committed, people tend to stick to their decision even when it becomes less attractive.

questions.prompt: Asch's participants conformed despite seeing the correct answer. This suggests mainly:
questions.explanation: When writing answers privately, conformity fell, suggesting a desire to fit in.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the foot-in-the-door technique.
items: Person's self-image shifts towards being helpful
questions.explanation: Consistency with the earlier commitment increases compliance.
